newsitem.title: UK: Sugar - Heavy rains still hamper East Europe beet.
newsitem.headline: Sugar - Heavy rains still hamper East Europe beet.

text.p: The weather remains crucial for eastern Europe's 1996/97 beet crop with sugar production still expected to be lower than last year despite patchy recovery.
In its first estimate of world 1996/97 sugar production, statistician F.O. Licht said east European output should fall to 9.29 million tonnes after the 9.71 million notched up last year.
Output was expected to fall sharply in Ukraine and Russia but the Czech Republic and Poland expect higher crops, it said.
In Ukraine, the largest producer, farmers are seeing long harvest delays with only 10 percent of beets lifted.
A severe fuel shortage has been blamed for much of the delay and only 14,000 of 18,000 combines were in working order.

Work in the fields should be completed in October and beets brought to refineries during November. Industry officials said the warm weather forecast for much of this month should spur the harvest, which began two weeks late to allow more beet growth.

"All sugar producers' hopes are pinned on the weather," said Leonid Bershtein, a deputy director of Ukraine's Sugar Research Institute. "If we have frosts in the last half of October there will be significant losses," said state concern Ukrtsukor deputy head Olexander Bohatarenyk.
The Ukrainian government has forecast a poor beet harvest of 26 million tonnes, down from last year's 30 million.
Russia still looks on course for lower sugar output this year despite a slight improvement in the weather.
"For two or three days we've had no rains, which is good," said Viktor Sukhachyov, deputy head of the Rossakhsvyokla beet producers association on Monday.
But he added it would produce below 1.6 million tonnes of refined sugar from its crop, less than a third of annual demand.
Last week, Sukhachyov said Russia's beet harvest would be 16 million tonnes, not 17.1 million as previously estimated.

"If conditions are not favourable -- rain and frost -- then even that level may not be reached," he said. "There has been rain in many areas, but most importantly, our equipment is getting worse and worse."
Last year's official harvest figure was 19.1 million tonnes.
Poland should turn out more sugar this year but wet weather may keep sugar content down.

"It's hard to estimate this year's sugar output because beets need sunny weather in September to increase sugar content, but this year's September was cool and rainy," said Alicja Banasik, an official of the sugar beet planters' union.
"The sheer size of this year's beet crop nearly guarantees that sugar output will top two million tonnes," Banasik said.
Poland produced about 1.6 million tonnes of sugar in 1995.
Poland's first beet test, on September 2, showed average sugar content down on 1995 but average root weights were higher.
In the Czech Republic, wet weather is hampering the harvest and causing lower sugar contents, so some refiners are starting to consider earlier yield estimates as too optimistic.
"It was expected there would be warmer weather in September, which did not come. Minimum sunshine reduced forecasts," said Jiri Janda, director of refiner Prazska Cukerni Spolecnost.
Janda said beet yield per hectare was likely to be slightly above last year but lower than earlier forecasts. "Contamination (with mud) is high, it ranges around up to 20 percent."
If wet weather continues losses on fields will rise and the final result will be much lower than originally expected, he said, but added the campaign would cover local demand.
In the late summer, industry analysts forecast Czech white sugar output at over 500,000 tonnes after 460,035 last year.
In Slovakia, the Statistical Bureau said rain was affecting sugar content. But rain earlier in the year benefitted the crop which was expected to be 38.1 percent up on last year.

Hungary expects a higher crop with some surplus beets likely to be exported. "Although sugar content per beet is relatively low, this is offset by higher than expected root weight due to almost permanent rains since mid-August," said Andras Angeli, chairman of the Sugar Industry Association.
Heavy rain delayed harvesting but factories would gear up to full capacity this week as fields dried out.
Bulgarian white sugar production is expected to fall to 7,100 tonnes this year, less than half of last year, due to lower yields caused by bad weather and scarce funds.
"The estimated sugar beet yield will be catastrophically low," Sugar Institute director Botyo Mitev told Reuters.
Farmers found it hard to obtain funding due to the economic crisis and only two of the seven refiners were operating.

Yugoslavia's Statistics Office said sugarbeet output would rise 38 percent to 2.34 million tonnes and average yield was expected to be 33.6 tonnes per hectare, up 6.2 tonnes from 1995. --Compiled in London with contributions from Kiev, Moscow, Warsaw, Prague, Bratislava, Budapest, Sofia and Belgrade.
